utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber received a message that both Defence teams had preliminaries to be raised. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. The first thing is a Stanisic-alone issue which relates -- perhaps we could, with Your Honour's leave, go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The next issue is a joint issue and it's an application to adjourn the cross-examination of the next witness on the basis of firstly late disclosure of statements which we -- a statement which we submit ought to have been disclosed pursuant to Rule 66(A)(ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that statement being?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: A interview that the witness had with the Canadian police dated the 2nd and 3rd of June, 2004. And that interview consists of two parts, one dated the 2nd of June, 2004, and the second part dated the 3rd of June, 2004. We were disclosed those statements yesterday. However, the 3rd of June, 2004 interview appears incomplete and has a large portion of it only in B/C/S. We would like a greater opportunity to read that interview and we would also like an interview to have the remainder of the interview translated. The second part of the application rests on the non-possession of this witness's testimony in the Belgrade court in November 2003 when the witness testified in the case of former Skorpion member Sasa Cvetan. This interview came to light -- sorry, this testimony came to the attention of the Defence when we were going through the voluminous disclosure relating to this witness, and this witness spoke about that testimony, and importantly claimed to have lied in that testimony due to pressure or threats or attempts to persuade him to lie by former members of the Skorpions. Thereafter, the witness claims to have told the truth in subsequent proceedings in Belgrade. The application, therefore, is to hear the direct examination and then be given a reasonable opportunity to examine the late disclosure, and we do submit there was a disclosure violation. The interview of the 2nd and 3rd of June, 2004, we submit, falls squarely within Rule 66 and ought to have been disclosed promptly. And we would like the opportunity from the English speaking team or largely English speaking team, we would like the opportunity to read that interview in English. But in our submission, perhaps the strongest part of the application is the second part, and we submit that it is absolutely essential to see what this witness admits to have lied about in his testimony in November of 2003 to be able to examine those lies and presumably the witness will claim some truths in light of the disclosure which followed. For Your Honours' information, we in the Stanisic Defence will advance the case that this witness continues to lie, in particular in connecting the DB in the way he does to the Skorpion group and also in relation to what the witness attempts to do in connecting the DB to other military groups. And so there is going to be a full confrontation where we allege the witness is fabricating evidence for whatever motive or whatever personal motive he might have. And we submit the witness -- a witness of this kind when put forward by the Prosecution ought to be put forward as a witness of truth with the Prosecution providing the full totality of what the witness has said on the subject, and with the Prosecution making it clear what their position is in relation to that evidence, whether they seek to rely upon parts of that evidence, or whether they, in fact, perhaps take the same view as the witness that some of it is reliable and some of it isn't. But in any event, the position we are in today in our submission is that that analysis, whether by the Prosecution cannot take place, in our submission it cannot take place to allow the Defence a proper opportunity to prepare, and it certainly, in our submission, cannot take place in relation to Your Honours' view or assessment of this witness until Your Honours also have the full picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, under the present circumstances, I will not raise at this very moment the issue of making submissions on the delaying the proceedings because one of the conditions was that the parties would commit themselves to finishing this witness this week. So that is now a bit of a shaky condition, I would say, so therefore, let's first look at this matter. But before doing so, I'm looking at the Simatovic Defence, is the Simatovic Defence, does it share the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our position is fully identical to that of my learned friend Mr. Jordash. We received the disclosure yesterday after the housekeeping session, so after 7.00 p.m. on a tape. And let me just add, Your Honour, I know that court time is precious and that there's a danger of us losing two of those days, however, there are some, I think, eight or nine witnesses of the Prosecution left. Now, I didn't have time to go through the statement which has 140 pages with my client and discuss it, and my client is entitled to adequate defence and a fair trial. Please bear this in mind. Given the circumstances and the coming winter recess, there's simply no time to read the statement with the accused. Thank you, Your Honour, I don't want to take up any more time. For the rest, I subscribe to what Mr. Jordash said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Two disclosure issues, the first apparently a Canadian interview 2004, the other one is, if I understand well, testimony in the Belgrade court 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me begin by addressing the Canadian statement. I recognise that it is something that should have been disclosed under 66(A)(ii). It was something that fell through the computer search cracks. It was not turned up in computer searches of our evidence collection. My efforts to investigate why that was indicates that it was handed by a judge in Belgrade to the head of our Belgrade field office and then was treated confidentially and wasn't treated in the normal way evidence would be treated. That was discovered yesterday in response to trying to answer a specific query by the Defence and it was disclosed yesterday. With respect to Mr. Jordash's concern that he does not have the entire interview, I've had Mr. Weber study the problem and he has just informed me by e-mail that the entire English interview is here but that when it was scanned in B/C/S it seems that some of the pages seem to have been shuffled. So although all the B/C/S translation is there, the numbering is a little bit out of order. We are trying to verify now that all of that material is contained in the report. With respect to the Belgrade -- proceedings at the Belgrade trial, I don't know that we even today have possession of what Mr. Jordash is requesting. He seems to be suggesting that we have an obligation to go and get the testimony that this witness gave in a proceeding before another court. I'm not sure that's the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. I would note, I've been informed by Mr. Jordash that it was something that was said in the Seselj case that indicated that the existence of this material, and the transcript of the Seselj case was disclosed on the 15th of September, 2008, so the Defence have also had notice of this document existing in the Belgrade court for quite some time, over two years. I would suggest, Your Honour, the following: I've read the Canadian statement. I don't see that there's anything new or substantially different. It deals with materials unrelated to this case, but there is a significant portion that does deal with issues related to this case. I would ask if -- that the Defence counsel be asked to address the Chamber on what the prejudice is. I'm not sure there's anything new in this document. But I do recognise that it should have been disclosed and I apologise to Court and my colleagues on the Defence that it wasn't. With respect to the Belgrade document, again I don't know that we do have it. I have someone who speaks the language. We cannot find it on our system. There is a file that we find on our system that says "Belgrade file," it does not specifically mention this witness. It's a very large volume of material. I have somebody at this very moment looking through that material to see if within that material is contained the statement or the testimony of this witness. If that testimony is in that file, then I would recognise that it was disclosable under 66(A)(ii). If it's not found in that file, then my submission would be that Mr. Jordash was under the -- had the same notice and had the same capacity and same time-period, two years, with which to secure that evidence if that's something that he thought that he needed before he could cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not sure we -- let me start again. I'm not sure that looking at the Canadian interview Mr. Weber has got it right on this occasion. It is a jumbled collection of testimony, that's for sure. And that supports our application in that being handed it last night at 7.00 or thereabouts and having to be forced to go through it at 6.00 in the morning at speed whilst trying to do last-minute preparation as well, is far, far, far from ideal, and I certainly do not feel confident that I've managed to look at that interview and properly assimilate it. I certainly have not had the opportunity to discuss it with my client, the most -- obviously the most important person in this Defence. In relation to the Belgrade testimony, I think the Prosecution's position is somewhat unfair. This is a witness who the Prosecution have spoken to on many, many, many occasions. There are at least just from the top of my head eight or nine different occasions when the Prosecution must have spoken to him. Three trials, various statements, more statements than for any witness in this trial so far. And in our submission it's hard to understand how given that volume of interviewing, given the issues that have arisen during that -- those interviews concerning the witness's protective measures, given the witness's assertions through these statements about lying in the Belgrade court, it's somewhat surprising that the Prosecution have not had possession of that testimony. In our submission it's likely that they do, it's likely it's there somewhere, and it's likely that it will turn up. In our submission whether that's correct or not, whether the Prosecution, it turns out, do not have it, whether the Defence ought to have approached the Belgrade court to find it, the situation is that this is a Prosecution witness put forward to give extremely contentious evidence, and in our submission to be asked to cross-examine without what might turn out to be the principal testimony which allows proper impeachment, in our submission would be an exercise in futility. To be asked to cross-examine the witness without the very testimony which the witness now resiles from, in our submission, would be to cross-examine him with our hands behind our back. In our submission, a witness such as this ought to be approached with substantial caution as befits the reliance that the Prosecution want the Chamber to place upon his testimony, and that caution, in our submission, involves adjourning his cross-examination to allow all of his testimony to be in front of the Chamber and in the hands of the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Any need to further responds, Mr. Groome, or has everything been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only thing I would add, Your Honours, I'm not sure it has to be all or nothing. I don't see why we couldn't proceed and go as far as we can with the cross-examination, and I certainly would not oppose if Mr. Jordash or Mr. Bakrac made the request that the witness be recalled, I certainly would not oppose it based upon attainment of new material whether it's my fault or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, I take it that from your previous submission that that is exactly what you want to avoid to happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I understood you well. Now, as far as the Canadian statement is concerned, of course the Chamber could not look at the Belgrade because it's -- at least the Prosecution says they don't have it. Whatever is available of course we would like to know so in order to consider your application.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Perhaps what I could also do is to find the -- at least some of the references to the testimony in the statements that you do have, so Your Honours can see how the issue was dealt with by this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have not paid specific attention to it in this context as a matter of fact. Then another matter, Mr. Groome, perhaps you could help me because you certainly would have studied that rule. The rule on late disclosure is?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The rule on disclosure, Your Honour, or the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The later disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Wait just one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you have to, at least the rule as I remember it, was that you would have to disclose it to the Chamber as well, if it's late disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that aspect of the rule, Your Honour, that the Prosecution would have a disclosure obligation to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's late disclosure if you have not met your disclosure obligations. So let me just have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yeah, I do see that, Your Honour. It's Rule 67(D).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 67(D), let me just have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If either party discovers additional evidence or material which should have been disclosed earlier pursuant to the rules, that party shall immediately disclose that evidence or material to the other party and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So my recollection of the rules is still adequate. Now, 67(D) requires immediate disclosure also to the Trial Chamber, which under circumstances can be prejudicial to the accused because if it is incriminatory evidence, then the Chamber would see that already before it even has been tendered or admitted. Therefore if you want the Chamber to look at this material, and Mr. Jordash and Mr. Bakrac, there is a duty for the Prosecution to disclose it to the Chamber, would you, in view of what you've seen until now, would you have any problem in the Prosecution fulfilling this obligation under the rules? I am addressing both Defence teams. There is a duty which apparently has not yet been met, and as I said before, I consider the rule in it its effect could in the circumstances be prejudicial to the accused because if it's incriminating evidence then it would come under the eyes of the Chamber even before it has been tendered. At the same time, if you want us to decide on the issue you raised, we might want to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We have no problem with Your Honours seeing it. It would make sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So under the present circumstances the Defence considers it appropriate that the Prosecution fulfills its duty under Rule 67(D), and Mr. Bakrac, I see you are nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Even before Mr. Jordash spoke, I believe that you noticed me nodding my head in agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's now on the record as well. Then the request is to delay the cross-examination, which means that we could start with the examination-in-chief. The Chamber meanwhile will have an opportunity perhaps to see that Canadian statement. Mr. Groome, may I take it that an on-going effort is made to see whether you have the Belgrade material in your possession?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Someone is examining the file now. My experience does suggest, Your Honour, that even if we do discover the statement of this person within that larger file that it wouldn't be translated because I think that certainly would have popped up. So I think if we do it, it's unlikely that it would be translated, but I should have more information at the first break. Mr. Laugel is in the process of e-mailing the Canadian statement, and if is assists the Court, I have an unmarked hard copy here in the court that I'm willing to give up to the Chamber if, again, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if we hear the testimony of the witness, we might not be able to read statements at the same time, although multitasking seems to be what we are all expected to do nowadays. Any other matter to be raised before the witness appears? Then under those circumstances, Mr. Jordash, I would like to delay the decision of the Chamber on -- and perhaps you have already prepared written submissions. I do not know whether there was any initial agreement between the parties that you would raise your request for delay of the proceedings four weeks after the end of the winter recess, whether you had made up your mind already as whether you wished to orally present it or to file it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We were hoping to make it orally, but events might have overtaken us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then perhaps we leave the matter for a moment. We'll see whether there will be any time. If not, of course, you are expected to make written submissions without delay. Of course, one of the issues is we don't want to lose time on this matter. If we wait for another day, then the Prosecution will have -- might have difficulties in responding to your request. At the same time, I do know that even if there's recess and even if none of the Judges are still in The Hague, they sometime become aware of filings, read them, and communicate about them. So therefore even if the recess would have started, then that doesn't mean that all communication and all decision-making is frustrated by that alone. If there's no other matter, then, Mr. Groome, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution called Goran Stoparic. There are no protective measures, Your Honour, with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Laugel informs me that he has just disclosed that material to Chamber staff. He has not cc'd the Defence, but I'd just let them know that that has been done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic, I take it. Before you give evidence in this court the rules require that you make a solemn declaration, and I'd like to invite you to make that declaration. The text is handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stoparic. Please be seated. Mr. Stoparic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic, could you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Stoparic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you a member of a paramilitary group based in Djeletovci, Croatia, known as the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's your best recollection of when you became a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely sure. I've forgotten in the meantime. It was in late 1992 or early 1993, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how long were you a member of that unit, or when did you leave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I left the unit in the spring of 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what month? What is your best recollection as to the month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection that was after we returned from Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 5884 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, while that document is being brought to the screen before you, have you provided statements to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY with respect to some of the events you have witnessed during the conflict in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you describe in some of these statements events you witnessed while a member of the Skorpions paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement to investigators of the Tribunal in November of 2003 signing that statement on the 24th of November, 2003?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we scroll down to the bottom of both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, you have two computer screens before you, would you take a look at the one on the right. It is a statement dated 24 November 2003. Would you please tell us if you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I recognise my own signature. I remember the date. I see my own initials there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the statement that you provided investigators of the OTP in 2003?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that 65 ter 5885 -- I'm sorry, Your Honours, could I ask that that be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the 2003 statement of the witness would receive?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5884 becomes P1702, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now call 65 ter 5885 to the screen. This is a statement dated 20 January 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, did you provide another statement to an investigator of the Tribunal on the 20th of January, 2005?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the screen before us we now see a statement dated 20 January 2005, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my signature on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is this the statement that you gave in January of 2005?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time could I ask that 65 ter 5885 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number it would receive is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P1703, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1703 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would ask 65 ter 5886 be brought to our screens. It is a document dated the 13th of December, 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being done, Mr. Stoparic, in preparation for your testimony here today, were you asked to carefully review both of these statements and review copies of those statements in your native tongue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After reviewing these two statements, were there corrections that you asked to make in order to ensure the accuracy of these statements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were your corrections recorded in a separate document, translated, and then submitted to you for review?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to once again look at the screen before you. Do you recognise the document now identified as 65 ter 5886 on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I recognise my initials. I read this document earlier today during the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this the document that records your corrections to the two earlier statements, the 2003 and 2005 statements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, if the Chamber considers your 2003 and 2005 statement in conjunction with the corrections that are now on the screen before us, do they have an accurate and truthful account of your evidence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now that you have taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the truthfulness and accuracy of the evidence contained in these three documents?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders P1702, P1703, and 65 ter 5886.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, the document you just said was -- the document you read earlier today, I think you saw one page on your screen. How many pages was that document that you reviewed today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that there were two pages in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you reviewed both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think that only the first page was shown to the witness, but as matters stand now, let's first have a number assigned to the document of today. Madam Registrar, 65 ter 5886 would received?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P1704, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1704 is marked for identification. Now, I address the Defence teams. P1702, P1703, and P1704, objections against admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's not an objection as such, it's just that I think we might have missed out the second limb required for 92 ter which goes into whether if asked the same questions and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did -- I do agree with you that it has not been explicitly dealt with. Let me just have a look, one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour, I'm happy to do that. It's an oversight on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, if the same matters would be asked, would you give the same answers as we find in the three documents taken together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, chances are that I might have forgotten things after such a long time in which case I would have a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you attest that when you gave those statements that you gave the answers to the best of your recollection in accordance with the truth, is that -- although you might not remember every detail at this very moment anymore; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? No. P1702, P1703, and P1704 are admitted into evidence. Mr. Jordash, if someone testifies being reminded of the solemn declaration taken that he affirms the truthfulness, then of course if he would have given different answers then he would have lied, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, and I was simply hoping to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no, no, it's appreciated. Mr. Groome, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would note the following with respect to P1702, the 2003 statement: It contains some evidence not directly relevant to issues in this trial, therefore the Prosecution does not rely on paragraphs 26 to 31, paragraphs 33 to 37, and paragraphs 41 to 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to now ask you some questions about the structure and operations of the Skorpion unit. I would like to begin by asking you describe the basic structural organisation of the unit. Can you describe that for us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You want me to describe the structural organisation of the unit when it was at its maximum strength? In that case, there were two companies, each company had up to 150 men. There was a reconnaissance platoon and there was a so-called work platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the overall Skorpions unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The unit commander was Slobodan Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was he also known by a nickname or a shorter name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did have a nickname which was Boca.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've told us how many people were in the companies. How many men or how many people were in the reconnaissance unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Things changed. Anything between 30 and 40, I would say. It depended on the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the structure as you've described it, was this the structure that existed in June and July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the primary mandate of the Skorpion unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Skorpion unit was based in an abandoned place called Djeletovci in the then Republic of Srpska Krajina which is currently the Republic of Croatia. Its main task was to safe-guard the oil industry of Krajina and that task also comprised the guarding of the 40 kilometre stretch of border between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. There was a natural border and that was a river called the Bosut river.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding your answer that the unit was responsible not only for safeguarding the oil fields, but approximately 40 kilometres of the border between Serbia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. The border between the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republic of Croatia, whereas you said the Republic of Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Where were the oil fields with respect to the border that the unit was responsible for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Most of the oil wells were located on our side of the Bosut river, on the side under the control of the government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were members of the Skorpions issued identification cards?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: All our officers and non-commissioned officers were issued IDs, red booklets with the inscription the Skorpion unit. The booklet depicted the person's name and the rank. And then on the last page of the booklet it said that the owner of the ID could use anybody's communication means or anybody's vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This last item in the -- in the identification booklet, what specifically did that authorise holders of this identification document to do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I will use my example and tell you what I did. At one point in time, I was manning the police check-point by the village of Njemci and since my battery had run down, I showed a policeman my document, he gave me his Motorola that I used to call my base.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did this document also give you the authority to use military communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, they're identical. I don't see any difference between the police and the military communications equipment. Actually, I'm not sure that I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think you've answered it, but just so that we are clear, did the document give you the same authority to use communications equipment used or in the possession of the army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember on the last page of the ID booklet, it said that we were allowed to use anybody's means of communication and anybody's vehicle, but it wasn't specified whether it could be only the police or the military or both. But I assume that in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we were authorised to use the communication means belonging to a military unit or a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your statements now evidence as P1702 and -3 describe some of the combat situation or activities you were personally involved in. My question is, during combat, active combat operations, did you and other members of the unit carry your identification documents into the field?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a policy prohibiting carrying documents while engaged in combat activities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We are talking about participation in combat outside of the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was not a rule. We had specific orders to leave our IDs behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Approximately how many vehicles were in use by the Skorpions, that they possessed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We had two or three vehicles, military vehicles. Those were actually lorries, 110 and 150. We had a Pinzgauer. I'm talking about classical military vehicles, and we had a Praga which remained at the base at all times. It was deployed at the sentry post at the base. We also had a Kula truck, we had a few jeeps, a lot I would say but their numbers changed. And there were civilian vehicles, Nissan Patrol and similar types of vehicles. We had a bigger truck, a pickup truck. We had quite a few vehicles of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did any of these vehicles have an insignia or name of the unit painted on them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The green vehicles, that's to say the lorries, didn't have any insignia, whereas all the other ones had the insignia of the Skorpion unit and the letters denoting that both on the sides of the vehicles, on the doors, and on the hood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What was the insignia of the Skorpion unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was your typical scorpion drawn, and at times you would have the letters saying the Skorpions on one side of the vehicle with the insignia being placed on the other side of the vehicle, and at times it would only say the Boca detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if any, licence plates did the Skorpions use on their vehicles when the vehicles were driven in the Republic of Serb Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When driving through the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, well, we had both the civilian licence plates and the army licence plates with the acronym SVK. We also had blue police licence plates. You could use them interchangeably on all the vehicles. You only needed to get a work vehicle log from the man distributing fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if any, licence plates were used on these vehicles when they were driven in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: None. We went without plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was there a reason why no plates were placed on the vehicles when they were driven in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: If there were no licence plates on the vehicle, I suppose that was a result of an order to that effect. Though I never witnessed such an order being issued. This is only an assumption. I suppose that the reason behind that was in order for us not to be easily identifiable at first sight. I don't know, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What, if any, licence plates did the Skorpions use on their vehicles when they were driving in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They would put up civilian licence plates of Belgrade and Novi Sad and M, that's to say blue licence plates. We had -- we kept various licence plates in the jeep in the glove compartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's the significance of what you are referring to as a blue or M plate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We had two such licence plates, one of them was M606 and the other one was M602, I remember those specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were any of the vehicles with the insignias painted on them driven in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the commander would go to Serbia frequently with his security detail every day, and at times he would have such licence plates on his jeep.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did his jeep have the unit's insignia or name painted on the outside?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: His vehicle? No. You mean if he had the large insignia of the Skorpions, no, no, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you have told us about the use of Serbian or blue M plates while driving in Serbia. Were these plates used prior to June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I know of these plates because I would frequently see the commander arriving at the base with the licence plates on. They were there before, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In paragraph 71 of your 2003 statement now in evidence as P1702, you describe: "In the JSO everyone had a red beret. In the satellite units only 50 per cent or so had the right to wear a red beret. Only instructors, commanders, and distinguished members could wear red berets." My question to you is, can you describe what you mean by the right to wear a red beret? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When the red berets are mentioned, one often times thinks of active JSOs. Well, they would undergo training and on the basis of them having completed training they would be entitled to wear a red beret. Whereas in the Skorpions, not everyone was entitled to wear read berets. Many of them wore black berets. It was only squad and platoon commanders as well as some other prominent members as it were, ordinary soldiers who would at all times be entitled to wear a red beret, and the red beret would then have a scorpion on. And if any of the other soldiers went around wearing a red beret, the commander was entitled to seize it from him. The story was that one had to earn that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you entitled to wear a red beret while you were a member of the Skorpion unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you instructed on a specific way in which you had to wear that red beret?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, instructed, any beret had to have been worn properly. It had to be tilted to a side and then above your left eye you had to have the unit insignia. Back at the time when I served in the JNA, we were told how to properly wear a cap as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 74 of your 2003 statement describes three different ways in which you received pay. I want to ask you some detailed questions about this. My first question --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to -- I hope Your Honours don't mind, but would it be possible to ask for some clarity on the time that the witness was referring to in relation to the wearing of the red berets. It's been left rather open in the statement and in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any problem in following this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash has asked me to clarify you some details about the time during which you were entitled to wear a red beret. Do you recall when as a member the Skorpion unit you were first entitled to wear a red beret?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Commander Medic was the one who gave me a red beret. Well, of course, for the first year nobody wore a red beret save for him. Now, I received my first beret from him in late 1994. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the remainder of your time with the Skorpions, were you entitled to we are that red beret?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I wore it whenever I wished to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when Mr. Medic gave you the red beret, was it done during the course of a ceremony, or did he simply hand you the beret one day to indicate that you were entitled to wear it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: There was a system in place. Every month when the best sergeant, officer, and private of the month was pronounced, he would be given a red beret and a CS-99 pistol.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter isn't sure of the designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you say again the type of pistol that was handed out at the same time as the red beret?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, we had two; CZ-99 and a small Magnum. He himself wore a sig sauer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say he himself, are you referring to yourself or Mr. Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Commander Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, returning to the issue of pay, my first question in this regard is respect to the money that you may have received from the Krajina oil company, can you tell us how often you were paid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The money that we received from the oil industry of Krajina came once monthly in an envelope and it was in German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there a particular time in the month that you received this money or did it vary?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: At times it may have been a day late, but I think that we would receive it on the first day of the month from the oil industry. And on the 15th of any given month we received money from Belgrade which was in dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you say you received money from Belgrade, how do you know that it came from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When the pay day came, it would normally be a delegation of individuals some four to five who would go to collect our money. We were told to wait for Manojlovic's return from Belgrade. We were told not to go home before he returned in order for us to be able to get our salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What currency was this money?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In dinars.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there anything unusual about these dinars?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, unusual, it was normal at the time to have always French -- fresh bank notes. They were always fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say "fresh," what exactly do you mean, and how did you know they were fresh?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you could tell that the money was new and the serial numbers were sequential.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, is that a convenient moment to take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a convenient moment to take a break. We resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we break I do have some information that the Chamber may find relevant. We have found some testimony of this witness in that file, it's in Cyrillic. It is not -- hasn't been translated. So I just would make the Chamber aware of that. We are still trying to determine how much of it pertains to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the Chamber has considered your request to stress and explain to the -- perhaps we should go into private session first.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, over the break we received the disputed record from the earlier interview of this witness from Serbia from Mr. Groome. Now, I would like to refer to the motion by Mr. Jordash for a delayed cross-examination which was a joint motion. Now, having looked at the record, I can say that the right to disclosure has in fact been violated. The Prosecution has had this document in their possession, and I suppose that they do have two related statements as well. I'll read them out -- read out the information briefly and tell you why it is important to have these statements disclosed. At the start of the trial it is stated that witness Stoparic has appeared before the court and given his particulars as he did on the trial on the 11th of November, 2002, which is a statement or evidence of his we don't have. Then at page 17 it is stated: "When the witness was confronted with his evidence of the 17th of December, 2002, evidently yet another testimony of his, the witness responded: 'What I said today at this trial is true. It is the truth that I experienced. I gave a different statement earlier on at the trial because that was how the defence lawyer advised me to do. Now I have a target sign on my back. I'm a big traitor to the Serbs, and of course I'm frightened.'" What follows from this is that evidently in some of his earlier evidence, Mr. Stoparic spoke some untruths having been advised to do so by his lawyer, but we don't know which portions were untrue, and if not for the substance of the testimony, at least for the credibility of the witness that it would be important to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I interrupted you, Mr. Bakrac, because you said earlier that the witness gave an untrue statement so advised by the defence counsel, from what I understood, and now a couple of lines later you say having been advised to do so by his lawyer. Now, I do understand that he was a witness in that case, so therefore I see at least I have difficulties in reconciling whether he was advised to do so by defence counsel, that this counsel for one of the persons who stood trial, or whether it was by a lawyer who would advised him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I -- perhaps what I said wasn't properly interpreted. I read what he said here: "I gave a different statement earlier on at the other trial because that's what the defence counsel advised me to do." In our system a witness is not entitled to lawyer when appearing in a courtroom, so it must be a defence counsel for one of the accused. Bearing in mind our jurisdiction, I'm sure that there must be a statement that Stoparic gave at the investigative stage which is yet another statement we don't have and that is prejudicial to us. This is an infringement of our right to disclosures and so we join Mr. Jordash's motion for additional time to prepare for the cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac, just suggesting that there may be another statement and already conclude that it's prejudicial to not give it to you where it has not even been established that it does exist, and just you think it would be likely that it exists, is at least taking the matter not step by step but jump by jump. Let's first hear what Mr. Groome wants to say in response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also have some information about this document, and I invite the native speakers on the Defence to correct anything that I say if it's inaccurate. It's eight pages, and they are notes by a court assistant. It's not a verbatim account of what the person has said, but it is some notes taken by a court assistant in a prior trial. Now, I've asked for the entire thing to be translated on a rush basis, and they tell me that we will have the entire document tomorrow afternoon. Having said that, during the break I had a native speaker kind of read it and give me the gist of it. My understanding is that this is a testimony regarding an incident in Podujevo, Kosovo, so it's completely unrelated matter, the substance, it's nothing that this witness is going to testify here. And if I could recall for the Chamber, Mr. Jordash last week when this topic came up actually objected to a question that I was asking about this saying that that matter was irrelevant. So I don't believe it's disclosable under 66(A)(ii). Now, having said that, if what Mr. Bakrac says is true, that there's some admission that he may have changed his statement about anything, I guess there is a reasonable view that it might be considered Rule 68. If Mr. Bakrac can indicate that specific portion to me, I'm quite confident that I could have that translated before we conclude today, and then all of the information that is truly disclosable, the Rule 68 material would be disclosed before the end of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could I first ask you when going through that statement very quickly apart from forming an opinion on what other statements that should exist, did you -- did you find that the statement or the testimony was given primarily in relation to a Kosovo event?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I skimmed through the document as far as the break would allow me, and I said a insofar as it related to Kosovo alone and not to this case, and I'm talking about three testimonies at least, testimonies before a court of law, they would be important for us because they would go to the credibility of the witness. We have a witness's own statement where he said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to tell you that it would have been appropriate to inform the Chamber in this respect as fully as possible and apart from forming opinions on other documents that may be in existence, to first of all inform the Chamber about not what may be the case, but what is the case and that is that this statement was at least about Kosovo. I'm not saying that for the credibility of the witness you might not have an interest in looking at other statements as well so as to see whether the witness has been consistent when giving statements, but this information which Mr. Groome brought to our attention is something we would have expected you to inform the Chamber about as well. Mr. Groome invited you to give the relevant portions and references so that he could do his utmost best to have the most relevant information accessible. I take it that you are willing to assist Mr. Groome in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour. I don't know if I'm expected to do it in writing or orally now, but if I can be allowed to explain first, when particulars were taken from the witness at trial, it was said that the particulars were the same as the ones given on the 11th of November, 2002, so we can deduce that he already testified. At page 17 when he was told that what he just stated differed from what he had stated on the 17th of December, 2002, well, then I conclude that there must exist a testimony of his which we don't have and for that one he said that it was untrue and that he gave it under the persuasion of the defence counsel. And I can give the ERN reference for my learned friend Mr. Groome. It's page 17, K0547120. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it may make a difference. I'm not saying that it's irrelevant. If the witness was not consistent in his statements about Kosovo, I certainly see that you might have an interest in establishing that. At the same time, if those testimonies were about the events which are vital for this case, of course the impacts would have been by far bigger. At least that's what you could presume not having seen them yet. It's all to some extent speculative, although some speculation is better reasoned than other speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I support Mr. Bakrac, and in our submission it's crystal clear and there can be no doubt that there are at least two statements which we don't have sight of because the statement that we have just been -- had disclosed to us in breach of the disclosure rules indicates precisely that. There can be no doubt about it. The one aspect which it might be speculative, but I doubt it, is whether there's a third which is that which arises from an investigation by the investigating judge as a precursor to the missing statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that we should explore what actually does exist as quickly as possible and as thoroughly as possible and what the outcome of such an exploration would be for the request to delay cross-examination is to be considered by this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, add two points and that's these: One, in the testimony that we have received, which relates to the Kosovo incident, in all instances there is useful testimony given concerning the -- how the Skorpions came into existence, command structures and so on. It's not simply evidence which is related to 1999. It's evidence which starts with the witness's participation in the Skorpion unit. And secondly, it's only right to correct Mr. Groome, when Mr. Groome led evidence of that Kosovo incident, I objected and on the basis of relevance and Your Honours overruled the objection. So for Mr. Groome now to say, well, the Defence said it wasn't relevant, I think we've moved past that point and it became relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you would consider that an inconsistent approach to the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Groome, before I give you an opportunity to respond because we are still talking about a request for the delay of cross-examination, perhaps before I give you an opportunity to, well, if I would say, to say the last word that would not be appropriate, but at least to submit what you wanted to add, one question: This material you found, is that part of the electronic disclosure system that is the Belgrade stuff, if I could say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do not know, Your Honour, I'm going to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please try to find that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you -- now you have an opportunity to make any final observation you'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The only comment that I would make, Your Honour, is I mean if it's disclosable and if I -- I don't try to avoid my disclosure obligations, I do my best to discharge them, but I seem to be hearing Defence counsel, their position, and I want to clarify if it is their position, it's my position that the jurisprudence places upon me the burden of if I'm in possession of disclosable material to turn it over. I don't see that the jurisprudence or the rules require me to go to the district courts in Serbia to obtain testimony and translate it of this witness in an unrelated case, or even -- I mean, I just don't understand that that's the obligation that I have. I think that -- I want to make sure that counsel are not under the misapprehension that somehow tonight or tomorrow I'm to try to contact these courts and obtain rush copies of the documents that they believe would be useful. My position is quite frankly that they've had possession of the Seselj testimony for two years now. If in reading that they saw something about a reference to a Belgrade case that they thought merited some investigation, I mean they were certainly free to do that. If it wasn't done, again if I'm in possession of it I have a duty to disclose it. If I'm not in possession of it, I don't believe it's my duty now to go and actively go get these documents before cross-examination can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I see that you'd like to add one or two words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only because Mr. Groome wanted our position and inquired upon it, but if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let's do it, but let's then in two minutes. I already asked the usher to get the witness and to be stand by at the door-step which --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I can deal with it in 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so, because Mr. Usher needs more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We take a position and the royal Canadian late disclosure, that's a violation, we take a position on this latest statement, that's a violation. In relation to the rest and the remainder at this point, until we see what it contains, we don't take in position, but it looks very likely that it may well have been Rule 68 material which, given the contents of this latter statement served today, may well ought to have been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you are thinking in Rule 68 terms of exculpatory rather than ideous [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Mr. Bakrac, may I take it that you join all the submissions made by Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting for the witness, if I could just clarify with Mr. Bakrac, my staff tell me it's the first paragraph on the page that he has referred to, and that's the one that we will try to have translated this session. Is there any other paragraphs on that page that Mr. Bakrac feels should be translated on an urgent basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the time being I can't see that. However, I will listen to the examination-in-chief. I will ask my colleague Mr. Petrovic to look, and as soon as we have the result, we will inform Mr. Groome accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you could send him an e-mail. Even if we are in court we can send and receive e-mails. Mr. Stoparic, you had to wait far longer than you expected, that was due to procedural matters which were raised in your absence. We are now ready to continue to hear your evidence, Mr. Groome will continue his examination-in-chief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I do, Mr. Laugel informs me that the document is not on the EDS system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, prior to the break I was making an inquiry about the methods in which you receive payment and you told us about two. Now, in paragraph 34 of your 2003 statement you say: "I received a third salary from Boca himself." My first question is, who are you referring to when you say Boca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Our commander Slobodan Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you now explain this third salary? Can you give us some more particulars about what it consisted of and what it was for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That was my personal agreement with Medic. Sometimes he gave out money and sometimes he paid us in kind in oil or petrol, in any oil derivatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did other members of the Skorpions have similar arrangements with Commander Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: A few but not many. Company commanders, some platoon commanders, as well as some men who were related to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 76 of your 2003 statement, now P1702, you state: "The order came from the top that 60 per cent of our men should be from the Republic of Srpska and Republic of Serb Krajina and 40 per cent from Serbia. This was so the people at the top in Serbia could always deny the link between the Skorpions and Serbia. They could always claim that these were Special Forces of the RS and RSK and that the men from Serbia among them were only volunteers." Are you able to give us a concrete example of something which occurred that demonstrates this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: On one occasion I got a call from the city of Nis, about 10 people called me and asked me whether they could come and join the Skorpions. And during a morning briefing with the commander, I told him that I had ten new men that had been engaged in the Vukovar front line. And then he told me what I stated in my statement, which is that according to an order, there shouldn't be more than 40 per cent of the men from Serbia, and the way he explained it is what I stated before you. And he did not allow me to bring those men in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that P347 be brought to our screens. At present it provisionally under seal pending a final determination on Serbia's request for protective measures. So I would ask that it not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, P347 is a document which lists payments made for the period between 16 to 30 September, 1995. In preparation for your testimony here today, were you asked to review these payment records?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to e-court page 26 of this document in its original and in its translation, and the page bears the ERN number ending 2955.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the original text, or I see it now, on this particular page of this document, did you recognise some of the names on that document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to tell us each one -- first tell us the number on the list where the name appears, read the name, and tell us how you recognise that person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The first one that comes to mind appears under 2, Goran Simovic. His nickname was Tralja. This is what I can add. We were members of the same platoon, that's how I know him. The next one under 13, that's me. I also know Jovic, Goran who appears under number 14. Number 15, Laza Kresovic, number 16 Zlatoje Bozic. I know a few more people on the list, their names ring a bell, but I mentioned only those men whose name I know and also that I can put a face to each of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, were any of the people whose names you've actually called out here in court, were any of them members of the Skorpion unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Nobody but me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, were you asked to review records for the entire period between the 16th of August, 1995, and the 15th of December, 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you see the names that you mentioned here on other payment records during that period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, do you know who General Loncar was?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I saw General Loncar on several occasions, and I know that he was the commander of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in 1995. And he was engaged in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe the relationship between Slobodan Medic and General Loncar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I never attended any meetings with the two of them, but I was present during their telephone conversation, and I could tell that Medic was rather arrogant, sometimes he used harsh words, even swear words. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Milan Milanovic, also known as Mrgud?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, he often visited us. I know him personally. That person followed us everywhere and he would take us to the field missions in Republika Srpska first and later on to Kosovo. He held a position in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina but I don't know what the position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you describe his relationship with Slobodan Medic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, Slobodan Medic simply adored him, and you could see that he looked up to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was there -- how did Medic treat him, if you can contrast that with how Medic treated Loncar? How did Medic treat the two different gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: When he was talking to Mrgud, he was standing to attention, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to the operation of the Skorpions in Trnovo in June of 1995. How did you first learn that the Skorpions were being deployed to Trnovo in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: How did I learn? I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Talking about prior to actually travelling there, did you learn before travelling there that a unit was going to be deployed there? And if you did, how did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Before we were deployed when we learned that we would be going to a field mission, I knew that we were being sent somewhere around Sarajevo, nobody ever mentioned Trnovo at that time, and I learned where we were being sent about a week beforehand. And I learned officially at a meeting one morning in Medic's office, Medic's assistant brought an official order from General Loncar, and I believe that the order arrived from Erdut. Srdjan Manojlovic was the man to brought that order to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was the -- how soon after receiving that order did you depart for Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We needed a week for preparations. How shall I put it, we were some kind of an autonomous unit in terms of food and other provisions. We carried everything with us. We didn't depend from any field kitchen, so it took us about a week to prepare all that, for the commander to assign which company and which men would be sent, would be deployed. A week later, in the evening we set out on the field mission. We entered Serbia near Tovarnik and from there we went to the village of Visnjicevo [phoen], and then from Visnjicevo we took a forest trail towards the bridge in the village of Raca. But on the other side, we were waiting for the night to fall in order to be able to enter Republika Srpska unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in your answer to my previous question on transcript page 46, line 10, when asked about when you learned about the deployment, you said: "And I learned officially at a meeting one morning in Medic's office." My question is, did you learn that you were being deployed unofficially --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, that's not quite the evidence. I don't think there is a closed quote. The statement goes on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can read the entire thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would please do so. If there's any dispute about whether it reflects or not accurately the evidence, this is the way to resolve it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll read the entire sentence start to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When asked about when you learned about the deployment, you said: "And I learned officially at a meeting one morning in Medic's office. Medic's assistant brought an official order from General Loncar and I believe that he would arrive from Erdut." My question is, did you learn -- you say I learned officially, did you learn of this fact unofficially at another time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, a day or two, prior to that we already knew that we would be deployed in the Sarajevo theatre of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how did you know that a day or two before officially being notified?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Somebody told us, but my memory fails me on that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember what organisation the person belonged to, if you don't recall the name?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Usually it was Milan Milanovic's line. He was the first one to learn everything. I am a bit confused. I really don't know what you are asking me. I know that -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not asking you generally. If you don't have a memory about when you learned unofficially, then I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to show a video-clip for you, and I would ask Mr. Laugel to prepare 65 ter 1167.4, a clip from the Skorpion video from time code 14 minutes 26 seconds to 16 minutes 16 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I'm going to ask you to view a clip on the screen before you from the original video of the Skorpion video, and I'm going to ask you a number of questions regarding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Mr. Laugel to pause at three locations during this clip. I would ask that he make the first pause at 14 minutes 33 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you tell us the person who is in the centre of this still holding a camera, do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who do you recognise him to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Stojkovic, also known as Bugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is he the person who actually held the video camera during the killing of the four Muslim men and two boys that appears later on this tape?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Laugel to resume playing the tape and pause at 15 minutes 9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Have you brought the chewing gum? "Ziko, the scarf."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We've now paused the video and we can see a person walking towards the camera that appears to have two things with white ends on them sticking out of his rucksack. Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what are the items that you have in your rucksack?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Rifle-launched grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What location are you in in this video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Somewhere on Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us some idea where that is in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It should be above Sarajevo. It's a mountain above Sarajevo. I don't know exactly. I never resided in Bosnia so my geographical knowledge of Bosnia is of a very general nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps I should have asked you, can you tell us where it is in relation to Trnovo? Are you able to tell us approximately how far away this location is from Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We travelled from the hotel you can see here across a forest trail to Trnovo and it took us several hours. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we resume playing the tape and pause one last time at 15 minutes, 15 seconds of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, we can see a man standing on an upper floor balcony looking at people below. Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's Commander Slobodan Medic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you know what he is doing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: He's overseeing our, well, unpacking, let's call it that. Soon thereafter we were supposed to line up and then he delivered a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would Mr. Laugel please continue with the remainder of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Did you tape it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is one of several clips that I will use with this witness and I have used other clips in the past. It occurred to me in preparation for this witness that perhaps better than tendering individual clips with various witnesses, it is my intention to tender the entire video with upcoming witness and that perhaps I would suggest to the Chamber that we simply mark the entire video for identification at this juncture and this way we can simply refer to the same exhibit but the different time codes on the original. That would be my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had some difficulties in following the time codes at this moment, but apart from the technical details, if there's no objection, then the whole of the video should be MFI'd for the time being, and then we sooner or later we receive an exact list, Mr. Groome, I take it from what has been played in relation to that witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the entire video would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P1705, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1705 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
