utterances.text: Your Honours, so the record is clear about the discrepancy in the code that we saw, whenever we create a clip, of course the beginning of that clip resets at zero, so all of the time codes that I have mentioned on the record here are from the original tape, and when the Chamber looks at P1705, the Chamber will be able to find those exact portions by the codes I've mentioned today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and it takes us quite a lot of calculations to verify whether what you say you play is really what is played. That's -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: From now on, Your Honour, we will be using the original, and then the time codes will correspond precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That will be of great help. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution is going to play 65 ter 1167.5. It is a video-clip taken from 51 minutes, 50 seconds to 52 minutes, 5 seconds of P1705 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask that we stop now. I've asked Mr. Laugel to stop at what would be 51 minutes, 57 seconds in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you see the green box in this video or boxes in the video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Or what is contained in the boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, what is contained in these boxes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: These are mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And how did these mortar shells get to this location?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We transported some of them by lorry and -- or rather, let me qualify this. We transported them a part of the road on the lorries and a part of the road on horseback.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that you look at one more clip today from P1705. It is taken from 52 minutes, 24 seconds to 54 minutes, 26 seconds of the entire video. I ask that you pay attention to the screen before you where you will see it played, and I have some questions after we watch it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "What do you mean for no reason? With a goal. With a goal of killing or disabling him. "And have you disabled him? "We have not, but they fired five shells on us. "They fucked us up good. "What do you mean they fucked us up good? Well, we fired but then we didn't fire after that since we saw that they had good co-ordinates. "Where are these co-ordinates? "Well, somewhere down there. "Whether that was an echo, well, let me light up, and Seca fired two rifle-launched grenades at them. "We fucking rattled them up."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I just ask that the video be paused at 54 minutes, 15 seconds, the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can see a man in the left side of the frame and he is lighting a cigarette. Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I ask that we play the rest of the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That was the first time in two days that we heard them fire a bullet. "I haven't heard it yet. "And then when you fired those rifle-launched grenades, they probably thought that we were going to attack them, that it was preparation. A rifle-launched grenade explodes like a 60-millimetre shell. What are you recording this for, motherfucker? "This morning those from Zvornik fired, but they fired somewhere towards us. Those ones over there? "Well, yes, from the right flank. "Well, no, they moved a bit higher, you know, and when they fire at this elevation here, if it flies over it hits you because they went around them, you know. "No. At the beginning they were halfway up the hill. "Now they have moved, you understand. Now when they fire at this elevation here in front of us, and when it goes over it, it hits us. "Seriously? "But that is high up. "Very high up."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, what are the green cylinders that we see on the ground in this portion of the video?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: These are containers or actually casings that contain the charge for a hand-held rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just prior to focusing on the cylinders there appear to be some type of weapon next to the tree. Do you recognise that weapon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to. That's a hand-held rocket-launcher and the cylinders are ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We can play to the end. I think there's just a few more seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "And grandpa is recording while taking a dump, eh? And where is he? Well, he is carrying some newspapers with him."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What types of targets would these rockets be used against?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, for anti-tank or anti-armour vehicles. They could also be used for the destruction of enemy fortifications, bunkers or emplacements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Finally with respect to this video, I'm going to ask that you take a look at 65 ter 1167.7. It is a demonstrative exhibit made from four stills from the 65 ter 1167.7. The stills are taken and indicated on the sheet as far as 52 seconds; 5 minutes, 35 seconds; 15 minutes, 9 seconds; and 53 minutes, 29 seconds. Can I ask that we start from the photograph or the still in the upper left-hand corner. Are you depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Moving to the right, are you depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Next to the priest, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the bottom left-hand corner, are you depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the bottom right-hand corner, is that you who fills the frame?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 1167.7 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1167.7 becomes P1706, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in the absence of any objections is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I ask now that 65 ter 3717 be displayed on the screens before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, once 65 ter 3717 is visible on your screen, can you tell us if you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I see are still the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's being changed now. Do you recognise now what is on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a copy of my military booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does your name and photograph appear on the front page of this booklet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The photograph was taken at the time I first received this booklet, and I was 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this document contain a comprehensive record of your military service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3717 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3717 becomes P1707, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence in the absence of any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that 65 ter 3812, a document dated the 12th of December, 1995, on the letterhead of the Republic of Serbia, Ministry of the Interior, be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you please look at the screen before us and tell us if you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It's a certificate confirming that from 11 June until 22 December 1995 I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia performing specific duties and tasks. I received this document at a base near Ilok which I believe is called Pajzos or something along those lines. At that point I returned my gear and the Erdut agreement was supposed to be in place already at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3812 into evidence as a public exhibit. Your Honours, the person who did the official translation of this document translated the period of service of Mr. Stoparic as being from the 11th of June until the 22nd of December, 1995. Given that the killings of the six Muslim males in Trnovo happened within this period, I anticipate that whether this document has been read correctly may become an important issue in this trial. Given its importance, I've asked investigator Ms. Pradhan to bring the original of this document from the evidence safe of the Office of the Prosecutor so that the Chamber may study the original document and the Defence too may look at that time it. I would ask the Usher at this time to receive the original from Ms. Pradhan and provide it to the Chamber and then to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to make any suggestions, but can the original in the B/C/S be enlarged for the witness to read what it exactly says, and I would like to draw your attention to the date of issue and its period of validity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there are two issues. The one is reading the handwritten portion of the document, and where a witness is not necessarily better able to do that, and then other elements which may be relevant for the interpretation of this original document, of course, can then be put to the witness. At the same time, there's nothing wrong with showing to the witness the detail of the document in this respect. Could it be given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3717 as a public exhibit. I'll -- I'm in the Chamber's hands whether the Chamber wants the Prosecution to retain the original or whether it wants to entrust it in the custody of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I looked at it from the computer, and if you enlarge the original on the computer, I do not see anything more in relation to the dates than I see when looking with my glasses to the original. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, if you switch on your microphone it will even be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was trying to but I wasn't successful. Your Honours, we do not oppose the B/C/S original being admitted into evidence because it's self-evident. We want -- we object to the translation being admitted because we are sure that there is an error in the translation which concerns a very significant portion of it. That's why I suggested if the relevant portion could be enlarged for the witness so that he could re-read the period for which the certificate or receipt was obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a translation issue, it's not a matter of admission, I think, but it is a matter of getting the right translation attached to the original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be heard on this matter. I haven't made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was just identifying what the issue was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess my suggestion, Your Honour, is that the issue is a little bit different than the way the Chamber has characterised it. I don't believe it's a translation issue, I believe it's a handwriting reading of the issue, has the translator looked at a particular figure and interpreted it as one number or another number. So, and as Your Honour has said, Mr. Stoparic has no greater advantage than any of us when we look at it, so it may be a matter that requires expert investigation, it may be a matter for the Chamber to ultimately find based on other evidence it hears, but I'm not sure that it's, strictly speaking, a question of a word being mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But since both the original and the translation says 11/06, the original and 11th of June in the other one, I wonder whether that was the issue Mr. Bakrac wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest -- I'm about to conclude my examination of the witness in the next few minutes. Perhaps it might be a better thing to deal with this outside the hearing of the witness, unless so that we don't influence --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify, Your Honours, and since you'll be deciding about whether we are going to cross-examine the witness or not now, well, I assert that it's 11th of August, but I'm sure that the witness perfectly knows if he became a member of the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia before that period or after. I'm sure that Mr. Groome can easily resolve the matter with Mr. Stoparic because Mr. Stoparic says in his statement upon return from Trnovo, I spent some time -- I apologise, Your Honour, but as I say, I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's -- one of the matters raised by Mr. Groome was that we should not discuss it before the witness. Perhaps we first ask the witness and then further discuss it, Mr. Groome, would that be -- would that -- wouldn't that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Again, I can, Your Honour, but I think as Your Honour pointed out a few minutes ago that he is in the same position as us. It's a number. I don't want to recite the evidence that could influence the Chamber's interpretation of it in front of the witness, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we could -- apart from the document, we could perhaps ask the witness questions about the matter which apparently also appears in the or is the subject matter of the document, but it doesn't make much sense - I would agree and I think that's what I said before - to seek the witness's opinion on what it says. But perhaps he has knowledge totally apart from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I'll attempt to explore it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, when do you believe that you first received money that originated from the state security service of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When you showed me the document several minutes ago, I read it fully and I said the 11th of August to the 22nd of December. In the documents you showed me, I found proof of it and those were payrolls because all the payrolls start with 11 of August and they end on the 22nd of December. And I -- I've seen 11 of June written here and I noticed that it wasn't right. Take the first payroll that you'll find with my name on it and you'll see that the date it bears is the 11th of August. It's illegible. It's been written poorly number 8, and I wasn't on the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia on the 11th of June, rather I was in the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You've used the term "reserve unit," now that's a term that Mr. Bakrac has used just a few moments ago. Am I missing something, I don't see where on the document it says the reserve forces. Why do you say reserve forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You are right, it doesn't say anywhere in the document, but I know that I was on the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we now go to -- Your Honour, I'll reserve my tendering of it until I conclude my examination or further discussion of it. I think that's as far as I can take it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me just see, the document we are discussing at this moment is 65 ter 3812 from what I understand. And you would like to have it marked for identification, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, until we can have further discussions on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P1708 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm also looking at the clock, I wonder even whether you should not more moments.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just have -- well, I have one more document to show the witness, but I can do that after the break if the Chamber prefers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that one document would conclude your examination-in-chief, is that what you intend to say or?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I just have another question that I want to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Altogether taking how much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we -- that you finish your examination-in-chief in the next five minutes. The Chamber will then decide on the request made by the Defence to delay cross-examination. Please proceed. Unless I'm looking at Mr. Stanisic as well because it's a bit longer than we usually do. I see that he is indicating that he -- he doesn't object to it. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, I want to read you a portion of your statement, and this is from paragraph 74. In it you say: "I was employed by the Krajina oil company and was given a high salary. In return, the Skorpions secured the oil facilities of the company. We also received a salary from the Serbian DB, and I received a third salary from Boca himself." My question is what period of time are you describing here when you say "we also received a salary from the Serbian DB"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the entire 1994 and 1995 our salaries arrived from Belgrade, and the man who distributed the money told us that the money had arrived from the MUP of Serbia. The oil industry had its own resources that they made available to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I now ask that 65 ter 3816, a document dated 13th of May, 1999, on the letterhead of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of the Interior be displayed on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, we can now see the document 65 ter 3816 on our screens. Do you recognise the document, and if so, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document. I received this document when I was awarded by the minister of the interior, and the award was bestowed upon me on the 13th of May on security day, the day of the security services. That's on account of the fact that I had been wounded and I had been very good at my job, and the job in question was fighting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija when I was a member of the SAI. I was a reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3816 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We have no objection but we would note that it does relate to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 3816 becomes P1709, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stoparic, my last question to you today is, and if I can return to your military booklet for a moment, it's now in evidence as P1707. You have told us when you were a member of the Skorpion unit. Is there an endorsement in your military booklet recognising your service in the Skorpions as military service? Did you hear the question? Do you want me to repeat it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there's no document on the screen. Am I supposed to answer without the document? I understood your question, sir, but I thought that we were waiting for the document. I can answer but I don't see the document. There is no confirmation at all in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you are able to answer without us calling up the document, then please do so. If you would like us to call up the document, I'll ask that that be done. Are you able to tell us whether there's an endorsement in your military booklet reflecting your service in the Skorpions as military service?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: No, there's no such endorsement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Stoparic, we'll first take a break and after the break the Chamber will decide on a request by the Defence to delay your cross-examination, so it depends on that decision whether we'll continue to hear your evidence at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I address you very briefly in the absence of the witness. It would take no more than one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whatever happens after the break, it's already break time for you. Could you escort the witness out of the courtroom, and we'll see you back anyhow in approximately half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I stood because I wanted to correct some information that I had provided earlier. In our rush to give the Chamber an answer about the EDS we were incorrect. In fact, the Serbian court case file is in EDS general collection under the ERN numbers that have been stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information, Mr. Groome. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I only wanted to add, if I might briefly, and highlight that the Prosecution have made Kosovo very much an issue now in this trial, that they produced an award relating to the witness's service in Kosovo. What the witness did in Kosovo now, and why he received an award is, in our submission, extremely relevant to the evidence that this witness has given and the evidence that the previous witness gave, and in both instances my learned friend for the Prosecution left it to the end of each examination to deal with this very much live issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any brief response to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The meritorious service does nothing other than go to the credibility of the witness. It speaks nothing about what he witnessed in Kosovo. If it were my intension to introduce matters with respect to Kosovo, I would have led from the witness another more serious atrocity committed by the Skorpions that he personally witnessed and has given evidence about. I have not done that, and I think that is a clear indication that it's not my intention to lead his evidence on Kosovo. I simply introduced a certificate he received for meritorious service while in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for what purpose exactly then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to his credibility, Your Honour. It's been already said here today; that is, it's the Defence case that he is an untrustworthy person who has lied. Certainly someone who has earned a high military honour for valour is something that the Chamber could properly consider in assessing their credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say because he received this award that supports your view that getting such a support would -- you would expect someone to be a credible person?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be one factor for the Chamber to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only reason why you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In our submission that is not what the evidence now leaves -- sorry, that's not the connotation of the evidence. My learned friend has led evidence of serious war crimes committed by the Skorpions in 1999 in Kosovo, they then produce an award, and the implication is that irrespective of war crimes being committed by the Skorpions, the Serbian MUP then gives awards. The idea that valour and courage relates in any way to credibility on the witness-stand is stretching the point too far in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 10227, there is an illustration of what my learned friend Mr. Jordash is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, do we understand you well that you would never use as an argument that such an award would show that people who may have committed crimes were nevertheless awarded and that therefore this is relevant information for criminal responsibility for those who may have issued such awards?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm not saying it's dispositive of credibility. I'm saying it's one factor that the Chamber could properly consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I asked you whether you would not use it as an argument in the way as I understood Mr. Jordash feared you would do. So therefore, it's clear what you now say you would use it for, but is it well understood that you would never in a couple of months from now, perhaps you would say, look at it, we have now evidence that heinous crimes were committed in Kosovo and now you see what happens, people who served in Kosovo were even award for their service there and therefore this casts some light on the attitude of those who are responsible for the operations of that unit? First of all, Mr. Jordash, did I understand you well what you feel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, the question to you now is if you say you exclusively used the document to convince us that awarded people -- well, not to convince us but this is an element which indicates or might add to being convinced that this witness must speak the truth because he is an awarded person. Of course I make it a bit black and white. But that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be the only inference the Prosecution would ask the Chamber to draw. The Prosecution is not seeking to have any other inference -- the improper inference which I think Mr. Jordash fears. And just to clarify what occurred with the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Improper or not, Mr. Jordash, you've now received a, I would say, a confirmation that what you fear Mr. Groome would use this document for, that he is not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that does deal with part of the problem. The other part is that the Prosecution themselves have asserted crimes in Kosovo are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's, yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps after the break. That might be better. We'll take a break and we resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will -- has considered the material that was disclosed 2003, 2005, 2006 statements. The Chamber has looked at, in the time possible, at the Canadian statement, which primarily deals with Kosovo again. Well, if I say again, that's wrong, because we had not anything yet, but the Belgrade evidence which is not verbatim evidence, is, as Mr. Bakrac told us, and as far as it could be verified is about Kosovo, whether there's other evidence which would cast a different light on the credibility of this witness, we do not know yet. That is therefore still uncertain. The evidence in the Seselj case, apparently we've seen that this triggered further requests from the Defence. On the basis of having reviewed to the extent possible at this moment the material, the Chamber considers that there's not sufficient reasons to delay the cross-examination of the witness, and we'll give the reasons in detail in writing of this decision. This decision does not yet cover whether at the end of the story, for example, for credibility reasons, there might be a need to recall the witness, but it's primarily based on the subject matter at this moment. Therefore, I don't know which party will be first to start the cross-examination, if it's you, Mr. Jordash. Then I would like to add to this that having resolved this matter, that the other matter, that is to make oral submissions on your request for four weeks suspension of the proceedings, now has to be considered again, whether you do it orally or in writing. Now, there is a fair chance that the procedural complications we had to face today might lead to the conclusion that there would not be sufficient time this week in court to make oral submissions, and therefore, unless you would come to an agreement this evening, I would suggest that the further submissions are made in writing, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Stoparic, you will now be cross-examined. The first to cross-examine you is Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Stanisic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to take you back to the time when you joined in 1991 as a volunteer, as a volunteer, as I understand it, as a member of the TO SBWS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that status lasted for a week before you received a military summons from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that you were amongst a number of men volunteering at that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And are you able to give us a picture of how many men, how regular it was at that point for men to be volunteering to that TO?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that there was a large-scale response. There were a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Hundreds or thousands?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav People's Army accepted volunteers at the time as well as the TO, so it's very hard for me to say. Hundreds of men volunteered.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And similarly to you, are you aware of hundreds of men thereafter receiving summons to report to the 1st Guards Brigade at the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Some did, some did not. Some volunteered, or rather, stayed voluntarily on the strength of some of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were there many of you reporting to the barracks in Sid to join the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, that was just a temporary arrangement. There was no military facility in Sid before 1991, but you can call that facility a barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you went to the barracks, were you given weapons there by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got an automatic rifle, an M-70.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you observe other men similarly being given weapons by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Members of my group received weapons, a non-commissioned officer unloaded a truck and distributed weapons from the crates. He made a list of everything that he distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And could every man attending receive a weapon from the JNA? Or did every man that you observed receive a weapon from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, everybody received weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you also observe taxi-drivers driving volunteers for free to the SBWS TO office which was in Sid around that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And similarly coaches driving volunteers for free to the SBWS TO office?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Volunteers would come to the train station. There they would find taxi-drivers, and some of them, not all, drove them for free to the town centre where the office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what would happen once they'd registered at the office? How would they, if their intention was to go to the front, how would they be processed from thereafter?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I can share my example with you. I don't know what happened to the others. I can tell you how I was treated when I reported, when I volunteered at that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please briefly, if you would.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: They took my particulars, my first and last names. They wanted to inspect my military booklet. In the military booklet there is a description of war assignment. They were not allowed to accept volunteers with a war assignment because it was never known when or it was not known when could the JNA mobilise such persons. If somebody did not have a war assignment recorded in their military booklet, they would receive a piece of paper. We would go to the temporary military base, we would hand it over there. We stayed there for a couple of days, we were trained and equipped with weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how would you be taken to the front? Where was that front at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The temporary barracks was located at the exit from the town of Sid, and my first engagement or my first front line was the village of Tovarnik which is about 5 kilometres away from the barracks. Half the way we travelled on a Pinzgauer and the other half we crawled to the village. We approached the village secretly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, which village did you approach secretly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And why was that? Why was it done secretly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, why? Because we were on a mission to attack that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Did you -- just to summarise and so that I understand the situation correctly, at the time you began and were recruited by the JNA, was it right that everyone you met received their weapons either from the JNA or from the TO in Sid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know actually. Or perhaps I didn't understand your question. All those I knew -- are you asking me whether they all received weapons from the JNA or the TO?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Was that where the people you knew received their weapons from?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I believe that we had all received our weapons from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that at the time -- and which period exactly are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that at the time there were strict controls as to who could carry weapons in and out of the SBWS region from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't go out that often, and whenever I did go out and then return, it had all been organised and arranged. I don't know who checked, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: And -- I apologise. There were probably checks for weapons if anybody was travelling on their own individually. I always travelled as part of an organised arrangement. Whenever we returned from the battlefield, the military police would be checking to see anybody had stolen anything or something of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand the situation. If you were travelling in JNA uniform in an organised fashion, could you travel from Serbia into the SBWS with your weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: That was precisely how I got in from Serbia, carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And if on the other hand you were travelling in as an individual or a small number of individuals carrying weapons, you would be stopped by the military police or the civilian police; is that what you observed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Since I hail from Sid and it is located quite close to the region, I would receive furlough for a day or two to go back home and would receive a permit for free movement which would state the quantity and types of weapons I carried. Without such a permit, one could not carry weapons to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And the permit would state that you were a member of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the permits were issued by the JNA and solely those issued by the JNA were valid, even if a TO structure were to issue such a permit, it had to be validated by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So in absence of validation by the JNA, you can confirm that the civilian or the military police were stopping and seizing weapons, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about 1991 or in general? If we are talking in general terms, I did see for myself on a couple of occasions when some of my colleagues who travelled together with me were -- had their weapons seized by the policemen or even in some cases were taken into custody or arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when you say in general terms, when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: When I say in general terms I mean from 1991 through to the end of 1992 at a time when there was fierce fighting in the region. After the fall of Vukovar when more peaceful times settled in, I don't think there were many volunteers left there anymore. The point you are trying to make is whether there were check-points along the border, yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what -- I just want to be clear then we can move on. From 1991 through to the end of 1992 there was check-points, from what you observed, were stopping volunteers who were not certified as a member of the JNA, stopping, searching, and removing weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: What I know is that the most rigorous check-point of that sort was in Baranja. The one next to Sid was not that rigorous. There was a large check-point near Belgrade at Simanovci where strict checks were carried out. I suppose there were other check-points, but I didn't take all the roads in that area so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what -- for what reason -- let me start that again. Did you identify a reason why the check-point at Sid was not as rigorous as the others?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Not always, but in the early days of September, October, and November 1991, it wasn't that rigorous because there was a very high level of traffic of the army crossing that point, and when I tell you how rigorous it was, well, I'm telling you what people told me, that it was less rigorous than the check-point in Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P1703 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a comment you make concerning the actions of the local court in Sid. Do you recall that evidence? About the local court not taking actions against individuals from -- who left the territory of Sid or those who within Sid committed crimes against Croats? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know of a single case at the time and I truly don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And how significant was the SRS -- the Seselj's party in Sid at that point in terms of its influence on the authorities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Without any doubt it was the socialist party that was the most powerful party. The SRS was a small party which only at a later date had some authority in Sid. I don't know how far that authority went and I can't express it in percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were -- is this right, employed or worked for at least the Municipal Board in Sid after the fall of Vukovar in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You mean the Municipal Board of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Serbian Radical Party and a member of the Municipal Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what was the role of the Municipal Board?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, party related activities. Preparation for elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there interaction with the JNA between the Municipal Board and the authorities of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Between the Municipal Board and the JNA, I don't think so, but there was between the Main Board and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, what is the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The Main Board of the Serbian Radical Party in Belgrade. They had relations with the JNA. As far as I remember -- well, the Main Board also set up a Crisis Staff, and as far as I remember it was Ljubisa Petkovic who was charged with liaising with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that liaising with the JNA something which occurred throughout 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: In 1992 I was sent out into the field or perhaps on two occasions as organised by the SRS. I would go to Belgrade where Ljubisa Petkovic would take us to the Boban Potok Barracks where we would undergo short training, some test firing, and from there we would be deployed to the theatre of war. On one occasion it was by plane and on the other by bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that barracks was a JNA facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the plane involved was a JNA plane?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: We were taken out to the field by a military plane and returned from Banja Luka on a civilian plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, what other form of liaising with the JNA took place? Are you able to give a little more detail about the Main Board's interaction with the JNA? Again focusing on 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA -- or, I am sorry, not the JNA, the Serbian Radical Party organised volunteers, drew up lists of them, and took them to Belgrade all together in organised fashion and placed them at the disposal of the JNA. If the JNA needed men, the SRS would organise these volunteers and deploy them to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And whilst you worked for the 1st Guards Brigade, you received a salary from the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't work for the 1st Guards Brigade. I was a volunteer within the 1st Guards Brigade. I did receive my salary, yes. I went to pick it up personally to the Guards Brigade barracks in Belgrade. I received my pay for the time I spent at the theatre in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, let me take you very briefly to some training that you underwent. You were trained, is this correct, just shortly before you went to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the actions in the villages of Tovarnik, Djeletovci --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the third village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- my group was sent back to Serbia to Sid to a place called Lipovaca which is a countryside resort. We underwent some sort of training there waiting for a certain amount of people to gather and from there we were deployed to the Vukovar front.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you were trained in part from one of Martic's police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: One of the four instructors was the only one who was a serious instructor who taught us something and he was called Giovanni. He wore a camouflage uniform with the emblem of the Krajina police. The other three were just Chetniks, nothing serious at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, when you were officially a member of the 1st Guards Brigade, what did you observe about the attitude towards crimes; specifically, was it very much dependent upon the commander of a particular unit and what approach that commander took?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: To give a picture of what it was like, the Guards Brigade had its active members who were in fact conscripts, young people who had to go through their compulsory term. They also had members of the reserve force and volunteers. We the volunteers could choose our own squad and platoon commanders. They did not impose their own officers on us. And that's how it worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that went for all volunteers, they could choose their own squad and platoon commanders? I'm focusing on your time during the Vukovar operations.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when I came to Vukovar from the Lipovaca camp, the instructor had already chosen me to be a squad commander. My platoon commander, a lieutenant, got killed in one of the first actions in Vukovar and that was when I was chosen to be the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, I want to just ask you about -- actually, just let me go back a little. How would volunteers choose their own squad and platoon commanders? How would they make that choice?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about Vukovar, it was already at a time when we were in the Lipovaca camp. The instructor chose the backbone, let's say, and then at some other deployments -- well, by that time the Vukovar experience had already made some sort of a selection. I knew from the start when I joined the volunteers that I would at least be a squad commander because of the -- of my comportment out in the field because of how I related to other people. And that was the case with others as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you act to prevent crime in your role as squad commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I was a platoon commander and I had four squads under me. I don't know what sort of crime you are referring to. Ordinary crime or war crimes? I did not see any sort of crime occurring before my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you say that it depended upon the squad or platoon commander whether crimes were committed by those under their command during the Vukovar operations?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: I am convinced that it all depended on the unit concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did it also depend upon whether the military police were in the locality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: You are right, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just going back, the training that you received prior to Vukovar, were you told about not committing crimes? Were you warned about it and educated in how to behave?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Nobody explicitly mentioned any sort of criminal acts, but I do specifically remember having been told that we should not hurl grenades into cellars before we call to the house and say come out. I can't remember the exact wording but that's what I did. Before I would gain entrance to a house that fire had been opened out of, you had to make sure if anybody was still in the house or not, and of course, the safest way of doing that was to throw a grenade at it. But before you did so, it was necessary for you to say, "This is the JNA, come out of the house." It is possible that because of shelling, people sought shelter in the cellar of the house. That's what we were taught.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you were directly trained to give that warning before entering a house, trained to tell the civilian, if there were any civilians, that you were JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: Explicitly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: The instructor said you don't know what urban warfare means. You have to get into houses, cellars, et cetera. In doing so, you will have to use your side-arms and grenades, hand-grenades, but before you throw a hand-grenade in an urban area, you have to say, this is the JNA, come out. If there are civilians around, they will most probably get out of a building. Soldiers probably won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock, can you wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I will, Your Honours. Let me just ask two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you in those circumstances also shout to civilians that you were acting in according to the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC
utterances.text: It would be very naive if we had mentioned the Geneva Conventions, but I remember that we used the term "law." We were supposed to say, "You will be treated in accordance with the law." There may have been people who also used the Geneva Conventions, but I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. I'll leave it at that. Thank you, Mr. Witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll adjourn for the day. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with anyone about your testimony whether already given or still to be given, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom because we adjourn until Wednesday the 15th of December, 9.00, Courtroom II.
